evidence_items.summary: Intraoperative bacterial contamination may contribute to microbial transmission during joint arthroplasty, but its distribution across surgical devices and clinical significance remain uncertain. This study aimed to characterize intraoperative bacterial contamination, compare contamination-positive and contamination-negative patients, evaluate contamination across device types, and assess postoperative infection outcomes. This prospective cohort study included 127 patients undergoing primary joint arthroplasty between February 2016 and April 2017. Samples from an unused control blade, skin-incision blade, deep-tissue blade, povidone–iodine-impregnated drape, and suction tip underwent aerobic and anaerobic culture. Patients were classified according to whether at least 1 specimen yielded bacterial growth. Patient-level characteristics were compared between contamination-positive and contamination-negative groups. Device-specific contamination was compared using generalized estimating equations (GEE) to account for within-patient correlation. Patients were followed for 24 to 38 months. A total of 13 of 127 patients (10.2%) had at least 1 positive culture. After exclusion of suspected sampling or transport contamination, positivity rates were 1.7% for control blades, 5.9% for skin-incision blades, 0.8% for deep-tissue blades, 2.5% for povidone–iodine-impregnated drapes, and 2.6% for suction tips. Patient-level demographic, surgical, and comorbidity characteristics did not differ significantly between groups. Overall contamination rates differed significantly among device types (GEE Wald χ 2 = 15.14, df = 4; P = .004), although no individual device differed significantly from the control blade; for skin-incision blades, OR = 3.65 (95% CI, 0.73–18.27; P = .116). No surgical-site infections, periprosthetic joint infection, or deep soft-tissue infection occurred during follow-up.

evidence_items.summary: Background: This study examined the relationship between microorganisms found on the hands, noses, and throats of music students and bacterial contamination on the wind and string instruments they use and evaluated the effect of cleaning on instrument contamination. Methods: This study included 34 students (19 flute and 15 string-instrument players). Swab samples were taken from participants’ hands, noses, and throats; from the mouthpieces, inner surfaces, and keys of the flutes; and from the fingerboards and bows of the string instruments. The effectiveness of the cleaning process was evaluated by comparing samples taken from the flutes after use and cleaning. The samples were examined using microbiological culture methods, and the isolated microorganisms were identified using VITEK MS matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry. In addition, the students’ participation in the orchestra and instrument-cleaning habits were evaluated. Results: Depending on the instrument type and sampling site, various associations were observed between bacteria on students’ hands and in their upper respiratory tracts and bacterial contamination on the instruments. As no fungal or mycobacterial growth was observed, contamination by these organisms could not be evaluated. Significant associations were identified between upper respiratory tract microbiota and instrument contamination in flute-playing students; following the cleaning process, pathogen growth was not detected, and microbiota growth was significantly reduced. Additionally, participation in an orchestra and habits of less frequent instrument cleaning were associated with pathogen colonization in the upper respiratory tract. Conclusions: Bacterial contamination varied by instrument type and sampled site. Routine flute cleaning was followed by marked reductions in detectable culture growth, particularly of commensal bacteria.
evidence_items.title: Bacterial Contamination of Musical Instruments in Music Education Students: Associations with User Microbiota and Routine Cleaning

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Next-generation personalized healthcare systems use wearable biosensors, implantable devices, telemedicine platforms, and medical IoT networks. These systems generate continuous streams of highly sensitive physiological data that must be transmitted securely across adversarial channels. Classical cryptography offers diminishing protection as quantum-capable adversaries emerge, while many QKD protocols use fixed defensive settings that cannot adapt when an attacker changes strategy. This paper presents the \textbf{Strategic Quantum Game Mechanism (\SQGM{})}, a quantum--agentic framework that embeds adaptive strategy selection inside QKD to protect real-time medical data flows. Two healthcare entities, such as a wearable sensor node and a hospital cloud server, adapt their quantum encoding operations in response to observed attack patterns. This minimises the quantum bit error rate ($\QBER$) while maximising the secret key rate ($\SKR$). The framework integrates an adaptive Bayesian defence module, a quantum authentication layer, and a lightweight Nash equilibrium solver for edge-deployed medical hardware. Evaluation on the IBM Quantum 7-qubit noise model and published QKD field-trial data confirms strong performance. \SQGM{} achieves $\QBER{=}7.1\%$, a $39.6\%$ reduction over BB84. It also achieves attack-detection AUC$\,{=}\,0.987$ and a 24\% improvement in secret key rate at 100\,km. These gains directly improve the reliability and confidentiality of continuous medical data transmission.
evidence_items.title: Quantum Agentic Secure Communication for Adaptive and Personalized Healthcare Systems

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents an LLM-enhanced ontology framework for explainable hardware-assisted cybersecurity in IoT/IoMT systems. The proposed framework integrates processor-level hardware features, including hardware performance counters (HPCs), device metadata, and CVE/CWE knowledge to support reasoning-driven malware detection and vulnerability contextualization. A hybrid human-LLM ontology engineering workflow is introduced to enhance ontology construction and refinement while preserving semantic consistency and reasoning quality. Using a top-2 AND SWRL rule over normalized HPC features, the proposed ontology achieves nearly 85% malware classification accuracy while linking anomalous readings to relevant vulnerabilities and device-context concepts. To support continuously evolving cybersecurity knowledge, we further introduce an Agentic Ontology Maintenance (AOM) framework that updates the ontology in response to newly disclosed vulnerabilities and hardware features threshold drift through a three-agent ReAct architecture with retrieval-augmented generation and automated validation. Results demonstrate that LLM-assisted ontology engineering enhances semantic reasoning and explainability, while AOM preserves logical consistency, competency-question coverage, and semantic quality across the evaluated maintenance scenarios.
